lesson.title: Pure and Simple: The AFL's New Model for Organized Labor
lesson.summary: As the Knights of Labor collapsed in the late 1880s, a rival federation built around narrowly focused trade unions and practical demands emerged to become the most durable labor organization of the era.
lesson.body:
The American Federation of Labor, or AFL, was founded in December 1886 in Columbus, Ohio, growing out of an earlier organization, the Federation of Organized Trades and Labor Unions, which had formed in 1881. Its founders deliberately built it as an alternative to the Knights of Labor's broad, reform minded, one big union approach, betting that a narrower and more disciplined model would prove more durable.

Where the Knights had tried to unite all workers regardless of skill or trade into a single organization, the AFL was built around craft unionism: separate unions for each skilled trade, such as carpenters, cigar makers, and printers, each retaining control over its own members, dues, and strike funds. The national federation coordinated support and lobbying but did not dictate to individual member unions.

The AFL's guiding philosophy became known as pure and simple unionism: a focus on concrete, immediate gains for workers, higher wages, shorter hours, safer conditions, achieved through collective bargaining and, when necessary, strikes, rather than sweeping social reform or cooperative ownership. Unlike the Knights, the AFL avoided formal ties to any political party or to socialism, preferring to reward political friends and punish political enemies at the ballot box while keeping the labor movement independent.

This focus came with a real cost. Because the AFL organized around skilled trades, it largely excluded the unskilled factory and mine workers who made up a growing share of the industrial workforce, and many of its member unions also excluded women and Black workers from membership. Still, its narrower, more disciplined approach proved far more resilient than the Knights' broad but fragile coalition, and the man most responsible for shaping that approach, Samuel Gompers, would lead the organization for nearly four decades.
